Uniform recurrences and complete mixed-linear order classification

Komorebi P. Final edition 1.0. 21 November 2026.

Abstract

We study Hankel determinants built from polynomially weighted central-binomial moments and first-order differential operators. For quadratic weights with the identity operator, we prove an explicit uniform constant-coefficient recurrence of order at most 63 and exhibit a specialization with minimal eventual order 63. For linear weights and arbitrary first-order operators, we prove a uniform bound of 112, show that it is generically attained, and give a complete finite algebraic rule for the minimal eventual order at every parameter over a characteristic-zero field. The classification includes zero parameters, repeated roots, spectral collisions, and their intersections. Exact portable certificates support the finite algebraic leaves of the proofs. The empty determinant is retained separately from recurrences beginning at index one.

This edition consolidates Theorems K, L, M, and N from the completed source edition. Its mathematical review provenance is project self-review. Independent review, historical novelty, and Lean formalization are unassessed.

1. Results, conventions, and reading guide

Let the coefficient field have characteristic zero. For the mixed linear family, fix four field elements and define

(E1)μ2m=u(a+bm)(2mm),μ2m+1=v(2m+1)(a+bm)(2mm),WN=det(μi+j)0≤i,j<N,W0=1.

These are the moments obtained by applying the operator D=u+v∂x to the even-moment functional with weight P(m)=a+bm. The elementary formal binomial expansion (1−4z)−1/2=∑m≥0(2mm)zm explains the central-binomial kernel. The proofs below work with formal Laurent series; they require no positive measure or endpoint integrability.

Write S for the forward shift: (SW)N=WN+1. An eventual scalar constant-coefficient recurrence of order r is an identity ∑j=0rdjWN+j=0, with dr=1, for all sufficiently large N. Its coefficients belong to the original field. The minimal eventual order is the least such r; order zero means eventual vanishing. It is distinct from the size of a transfer matrix or the degree of an unreduced candidate denominator.

Main result. Theorems M and N together determine the minimal eventual order of (E1) for every (a,b,u,v). Theorem L supplies a uniform bound of 112 and its generic sharpness. The reduced recurrences in the classification hold from N=1; the convention W0=1 is separate.

FamilyResultScope of minimality
P(m)=a+bm+cm(m−1), identity operatorTheorem K: uniform bound 63Sharp at (a,b,c)=(1,1,1); pointwise classification is not asserted
Linear weight, first-order operatorTheorem L: uniform bound 112Minimal order 112 on a nonempty Zariski-open set
Mixed linear family, abuv=0Theorem M: complete ordered boundary tableEvery zero-parameter intersection included
Mixed linear family, abuv≠0Theorem N: exact polynomial-gcd decision ruleEvery root multiplicity and spectral collision included

To classify a mixed-linear parameter, first test whether both weight coefficients or both operator coefficients are zero; the order is then zero. For every other point on abuv=0, read the ordered table in Theorem M. For abuv≠0, use t=b/a and q=(v/u)2, form the degree-four and degree-sixteen polynomials in Theorem N, and compute the stated gcd degrees and collision correction. This is a finite algebraic rule; it does not require numerical root separation or recurrence fitting.

The quadratic functional developed in section 2 provides the common proof foundation. Section 3 then treats general quartic functionals and derives (E1). Sections 4 and 5 complete its boundary and nonzero classifications, respectively. Section 6 explains the certificate logic and gives one-command reproduction instructions.

The letters K, L, M, and N, and their equation labels, are retained so the paper can be checked against the archived sources. Subsection references such as K.6 or N.3 refer within the corresponding theorem section. Auxiliary symbols are local to their sections: in particular, the polynomial coefficient q in K is distinct from the normalized ratio q in N. The normalization of R is restated whenever it changes.

The exact order explorer accepts rational normalized parameters and links to this paper. The theorem also covers algebraic parameters, including the order-64 triple-root case. Negative rational q is interpreted in a quadratic extension containing its square root; it is not a claim that a negative number is a real square.

2. The formal functional and the quadratic bound

K.0. Statement

Work over a characteristic-zero field. Put

P(m)=a+bm+cm(m−1),μ2m=P(m)(2mm),μ2m+1=0,WN=det(μi+j)0≤i,j<N,W0=1.

Let S denote the forward shift in N, and set

A=4a2,p=−8a+8b−24c,q=24a2−32ab−96ac+16b2,g(X)=X4+pX3+qX2+ApX+A2,k(X)=X4+4(b−2a)X3+(24a2−16ab+48ac)X2+16a2(b−2a)X+16a4,Γ(X)=(X−2a)g(X)k(X).

Theorem K. For every a,b,c, including all degree drops and the zero weight,

(K1)Γ(S)7WN=0(N≥1).

This is a uniform constant-coefficient recurrence of order at most 63. The previously certified specialization (a,b,c)=(1,1,1), or P(m)=1+m2, has minimal eventual order 63, so the uniform bound is optimal. Minimality at every specialization is not claimed.

K.1. A fixed formal moment functional

All expansions below are formal Laurent series at infinity. Define

ν[f]=[x−1]f(x)(x2−4)−5/2,(x2−4)−5/2=x−5(1−4x−2)−5/2.

Thus odd moments vanish, the first four moments vanish, and

(K2)ν[x2m]=m(m−1)12(2mm)(m≥0).

For m≥2, this follows by expanding the binomial series; both sides are zero at m=0,1. The elementary central-binomial ratios also give

ν[(x2−4)x2m]=m2(2mm),ν[(x2−4)2x2m]=(2mm).

Consequently the functional defining μj is exactly Rν, where

(K3)R(x)=a(x2−4)2+2b(x2−4)+12c.

This identity concerns formal moments; no positive measure or endpoint integrability is assumed.

K.2. Orthogonal polynomials after the singular initial block

Write σ=x2−4. For n≥5, define

(K4)Ln=(2n−5)!(n−5)!,pn(x)=σ5/2Lndndxnσn−5/2.

The derivative is σ−5/2 times a polynomial of degree n, whose leading coefficient is Ln; hence pn is monic. Formal integration by parts uses [x−1]f′=0, and proves ν[pnxj]=0 for j<n. Its squared norm is

(K5)hn=ν[pn2]=ν[pnxn]=(−1)nn!Ln(−4)n−2(n−5/2n−2)=2n(n−1)(n−3)(n−4)≠0.

The size-five moment matrix of ν is anti-triangular with anti-diagonal entries one, so its determinant is one. Changing the monomial basis to 1,x,x2,x3,x4,p5,…,pN−1 now proves

(K6)HN(ν)=2N−5(N−1)(N−2)2(N−3)2(N−4)144(N≥5).

In particular every required moment matrix is nonsingular, although the smaller initial matrices are singular.

The operator L=σ∂x2−3x∂x is formally self-adjoint for ν, since (σσ−5/2)′=−3xσ−5/2. Orthogonality and nonsingularity therefore give

(K7)Lpn=n(n−4)pn.

The monic polynomial solution is unique: the difference of the eigenvalues at degrees n and j<n is (n−j)(n+j−4)≠0.

Let x=z+z−1, dn=(n−3)(n−4), and

Fn(z)=znℓn(z),ℓn(z)=dn−2n(n−4)z−2+n(n−1)z−4.

Direct substitution into (K7), using ∂x=(1−z−2)−1∂z, gives

(K8)dnpn(z+z−1)=Fn(z)+Fn(z−1)(n≥5).

The right side is a symmetric Laurent polynomial, with leading term dnxn, so uniqueness applies. The direct substitution is also retained as an exact Laurent-polynomial identity in the replay program.

K.3. The transformed determinant, without an external theorem

For generic parameters write

R(x)=a(x−r)(x+r)(x−s)(x+s),r=z+z−1,s=w+w−1.

Here a,r,s,rs(r2−s2) are nonzero; excluded specializations are recovered in subsection K.6. The determinant identity needed is

(K9)WN=aNHN(ν)det(pN+j(ti))0≤i,j<4Δ(t0,t1,t2,t3),(t0,t1,t2,t3)=(r,−r,s,−s),N≥5.

For completeness, let Q=R/a, and let ν⊗N act on separate polynomial variables. Expanding two determinants shows HN(Qν)=ν⊗N[Δ(x)2∏iQ(xi)]/N!. Also Δ(x,t)=Δ(x)Δ(t)∏iQ(xi), because there are four added roots. Express the augmented Vandermonde in any monic basis in its first N columns and pN,…,pN+3 in its last four columns. After expansion along the x rows and application of ν⊗N, orthogonality kills every selection containing a last-four column. The sole remaining selection gives N!HN(ν)det(pN+j(ti)), with positive Laplace sign. This proves (K9), using no orthogonal polynomials below degree five.

Put Pn(r)=Fn(z)+Fn(z−1), and similarly at s. Parity gives

DN=PN(r)PN+2(s)−PN+2(r)PN(s),EN=PN+1(r)PN+3(s)−PN+3(r)PN+1(s).

Row and column operations give det(PN+j(ti))=4DNEN, and Δ(r,−r,s,−s)=4rs(s2−r2)2. Moreover

∏j=03dN+j=N(N−1)2(N−2)2(N−3)2(N−4).

Substitution in (K9) yields

(K10)WN=(2a)NDNEN4608N(N−1)rs(s2−r2)2(N≥5).

K.4. Nine bases and polynomial degree six

For u∈{z,z−1}, v∈{w,w−1}, define polynomials in the formal variable n:

Bn(u,v)=ℓn(u)v2ℓn+2(v)−u2ℓn+2(u)ℓn(v),Cn(u,v)=uv{ℓn+1(u)v2ℓn+3(v)−u2ℓn+3(u)ℓn+1(v)}.

Each has degree at most four in n. Since

ℓ1(u)=6(1+u−2),u2ℓ3(u)=6(1+u−2),

we have B1=0 and C0=0. Hence bn=Bn/(n−1) and cn=Cn/n are polynomials of degree at most three. These are polynomial quotients, including at indices zero and one. Expanding (K10) therefore gives the explicit exponential polynomial

(K11)WN=(2a)N4608rs(s2−r2)2∑ϵ,η,δ,θ∈{−1,1}bN(zϵ,wη)cN(zδ,wθ)(zϵ+δwη+θ)N.

Its nine possible bases are

λij=2az2iw2j,i,j∈{−1,0,1},

and their coefficients have degree at most six in N. Since (S−λ)d+1 annihilates λN times a degree-d polynomial, ∏i,j(S−λij)7 annihilates (K11).

Set T1=z2+z−2=r2−2, T2=w2+w−2=s2−2. From (K3),

T1+T2=4−2b/a,T1T2=4−4b/a+12c/a.

Expanding the four corner bases gives g, and the four axis bases give k:

∏i,j∈{−1,1}(X−2az2iw2j)=g(X),∏v∈{z,w}(X−2av2)(X−2av−2)=k(X).

The remaining base is 2a. Thus the annihilator is exactly Γ7.

K.5. The initial boundary

Formula (K11) also gives the actual determinants at indices one through four:

(K12)W1=a,W2=2a(a+b),W3=4(a+b)(a2+2ab+6ac−2b2),W4=8(a2+2ab+6ac−2b2)(a2+4ab−6b2+24ac−12bc−36c2).

These are finite Laurent-polynomial identities, obtained by inserting n=1,2,3,4 into the explicit polynomial quotients in (K11). After setting a=1, substituting b=(8−r2−s2)/2, c=(r2s2−16+8b)/12, and multiplying by 4608rs(s2−r2)2, both sides are Laurent polynomials in z,w. The replay checks every coefficient; homogeneity restores arbitrary a. Direct size-at-most-four monomial determinants give exactly (K12). Together with (K10), this identifies (K11) with WN for every N≥1. At zero, (K11) instead gives 1/2; the convention W0=1 remains separate. In particular the uniform start index cannot be lowered to zero when a≠0: the residual there is Γ(0)7/2≠0.

K.6. Every specialization and sharpness

So far the proof takes place in a generic extension where the displayed denominators are nonzero. For each fixed N≥1, the residue in (K1) is a polynomial in a,b,c with integer coefficients. Substituting the generic root parameters in (K3) is injective on Q[a,b,c]: the independent variables r2,s2 have algebraically independent sum and product, and adjoining z,w is algebraic. Since the residue vanishes in this extension, it is the zero polynomial. Specialization therefore proves (K1) over every characteristic-zero field, including a=0, c=0, coincident roots, singular moment matrices and the zero weight.

At (a,b,c)=(1,1,1), the factors become

Γ(X)=(X−2)(X4−24X3−88X2−96X+16)(X4−4X3+56X2−16X+16).

The exact reduced-OGF certificate described in section 6 proves minimal eventual constant-coefficient order 63 at this specialization. Thus 63 is the best possible uniform bound. Theorems L, M, and N below treat the mixed linear family.

3. The uniform mixed-linear bound

L.1. The quartic-functional theorem

Use the formal functional from the sharp quadratic proof:

ν[f]=[x−1]f(x)(x2−4)−5/2.

For any polynomial R(x)=r4x4+r3x3+r2x2+r1x+r0, let

μj=ν[R(x)xj],WN(R)=det(μi+j)0≤i,j<N,W0(R)=1.

Define C0(x)=2, C1(x)=x, Ck(x)=xCk−1(x)−Ck−2(x). For 1≤k≤16, set

Tk=2kResx(R,Ck).

Here the resultant uses the fixed degree-four coefficient list for R, including when r4=0; it is the polynomial determinant of its Sylvester matrix. Define

(L1)d0=1,dj=−1j∑k=1jdj−kTk(1≤j≤16),χR(X)=∑j=016djX16−j.

These formulas are explicit and involve only finitely many polynomial determinants and divisions by the nonzero integers 1 through 16. In particular every dj is a polynomial over Q in the five coefficients of R; no leading-coefficient division is required.

Theorem L. Over every characteristic-zero field, for every quartic coefficient list, including degree drops and the zero polynomial,

(L2)χR(S)7WN(R)=0(N≥1).

Thus these Hankel determinants have a uniform constant-coefficient recurrence of order at most 112.

L.2. Sixteen bases and degree six

The sharp quadratic proof already establishes the formal orthogonal polynomials, their nonzero norms from degree five onward, and the augmented- Vandermonde identity. Its determinant proof does not require an even R. For generic R=r4∏i=14(x−ti), put ti=zi+zi−1, and use its definitions

Pn(ti)=Fn(zi)+Fn(zi−1),Fn(z)=znℓn(z),ℓn(z)=(n−3)(n−4)−2n(n−4)z−2+n(n−1)z−4.

The same normalization gives, for N≥5,

(L3)WN(R)=(2r4)N4608N(N−1)Δ(t)det(PN+j(ti))1≤i≤4, 0≤j<4.

Expand this determinant by choosing ui=zi or zi−1 in each row. After extracting ∏iuiN, the coefficient determinant is

Qn(u)=det(uijℓn+j(ui))1≤i≤4, 0≤j<4.

It has degree at most eight in n. At n=0, columns one and three coincide, since uℓ1(u)=u3ℓ3(u). At n=1, columns zero and two coincide, since ℓ1(u)=u2ℓ3(u). Therefore Qn/[n(n−1)] is a polynomial of degree at most six. Equation (L3) is an exponential polynomial with sixteen possible bases

(L4)λϵ=2r4∏i=14ziϵi,ϵi∈{−1,1},

whose coefficients have degree at most six in N.

Their power sums are

∑ϵλϵk=(2r4)k∏i(zik+zi−k)=(2r4)k∏iCk(ti)=2kResx(R,Ck)=Tk.

Newton's identities therefore identify ∏ϵ(X−λϵ) with the explicit polynomial χR in (L1). To see the coefficient recursion directly, expand ∏ϵ(1−λϵz), differentiate its formal logarithm, and compare coefficients. Each degree-six exponential component is killed by the seventh power of its base factor. This proves (L2) for the generic tail.

L.3. The boundary and every specialization

The exponential polynomial extends to index one. The necessary boundary calculation is finite and uniform in the four coefficients of a monic quartic. For N=2,3,4, use

P2=4x2+8,P3=12x,P4=24,

and Pn=(n−3)(n−4)pn at n=5,6,7. Reduce these polynomials modulo R=x4+r3x3+r2x2+r1x+r0. If MN is the four-by-four matrix whose columns are the coefficient vectors of the remainders of PN,…,PN+3, the identities are

(L5)2NdetMN=4608N(N−1)det(ν[Rxi+j])0≤i,j<N.

All coefficients of these three polynomial identities in Q[r0,r1,r2,r3] are checked by both the exploratory symbolic calculation and the separate sparse-polynomial replay. The remainder construction is valid because the evaluation matrix is the Vandermonde matrix times MN; its determinant divided by Δ(t) is detMN. Homogeneity restores arbitrary nonzero r4.

For the boundary limit at one, subtract column zero from column two before dividing by n−1. The vanishing-column derivative has no logarithm of zi, since F3(zi)−F1(zi)=0 already branch by branch. Its sum of the two branches is

J(x)=−2x3+8x.

At N=1, the four columns are therefore 12x,4x2+8,J(x),24. Their coefficient determinant is 2304, giving 2r4⋅2304/4608=r4=μ0. At zero, subtract column one from column three; the columns become 24,12x,4x2+8,J(x), with determinant -2304. The additional factor n−1=−1 gives the exponential continuation value 1/2, whereas W0=1.

Thus the exponential formula agrees with the actual sequence for every N≥1. For each such fixed N, the residue in (L2) is a polynomial over Q in the five coefficients of R. The generic proof therefore specializes to every coefficient list, including repeated roots, degree drops, singular minors and zero weights. The uniform start cannot be lowered to zero when r4≠0: its residue there is χR(0)7/2=(2r4)112/2≠0.

L.4. Every linear weight and first-order operator

Let FP[x2m]=(a+bm)(2mm), with odd moments zero, and let D=u+v∂x. The induced moments are

(L6)μ2m=u(a+bm)(2mm),μ2m+1=v(2m+1)(a+bm)(2mm).

Writing σ=x2−4, the functional FP is (aσ2+2bσ)ν. Formal integration by parts for the derivative term gives exactly Rν, with

(L7)R(x)=u[aσ2+2bσ]+vx[aσ+6b],r4=ua,r3=va,r2=u(−8a+2b),r1=v(−4a+6b),r0=u(16a−8b).

Indeed ν[Qf′]=−ν[(Q′−5xQ/σ)f], and −Q′+5xQ/σ=x(aσ+6b) for Q=aσ2+2bσ. The quotient here is polynomial because σ divides Q. Theorem L applied to (L7) proves the uniform order-at-most-112 recurrence for all a,b,u,v, including pure odd, identity, zero and degree-drop cases.

At (a,b,u,v)=(1,1,1,2), the quartic is x4+2x3−6x2+4x+8. Formula (L1) gives

χR(X)=X16−16X15+384X14+1600X13−21568X12+129792X11+649216X10−2378752X9+9340416X8−9515008X7+10387456X6+8306688X5−5521408X4+1638400X3+1572864X2−262144X+65536.

This is exactly the reversed degree-16 generating-function factor in the published order-112 example. Its reduced numerator is reconstructed from the new formula and actual determinant values; the retained degree-preserving modular Bezout witness checks coprimality. Thus the uniform bound is optimal.

L.5. Generic minimality

The mixed-family minimal eventual order is 112 on a nonempty Zariski-open set of parameters. Here is the precise argument. Put

D(z)=z112χR(z−1)7,N(z)=[D(z)∑j≥0Wjzj]≤112.

The recurrence proves that the generating function is N/D. Both polynomial coefficient lists depend polynomially on a,b,u,v. At the certified sample they have degree 112 and are coprime, so their fixed-degree resultant is a polynomial in the parameters that is nonzero at that sample. On the nonempty open set where that resultant and the leading coefficient of D are nonzero, the reduced denominator has degree 112. Every eventual constant-coefficient scalar recurrence must annihilate that denominator, so its order is at least 112. The bound proves equality there.

Theorems M and N below classify minimal orders on the exceptional parameter locus. The bound 63 for quadratic weights with the identity operator remains the separate Theorem K. The broader scope is stated in section 7.

4. The coordinate boundary

M.1. Statement and complete boundary table

Over a characteristic-zero field, use

μ2m=u(a+bm)(2mm),μ2m+1=v(2m+1)(a+bm)(2mm),WN=det(μi+j)0≤i,j<N,W0=1.

The minimal order below always means the minimal eventual scalar constant-coefficient recurrence order. Order zero means eventual vanishing. The uniform bound 112 and generic minimality are established in the preceding mixed-family theorem.

Theorem M. Suppose abuv=0. If (a,b)=(0,0) or (u,v)=(0,0), the minimal order is zero. Otherwise the following table is exhaustive. Its families are read in order, so intersections are included.

The reduced recurrence in every row holds from index one. The zero-index empty determinant is retained separately. The two quadratic-relation rows with orders 10 and 22 have no nonzero real solutions for u,v; they matter over fields containing the required square roots of -1.

This theorem classifies the entire coordinate boundary. Section 5 classifies the complementary fully nonzero locus abuv≠0.

M.2. Smaller uniform recurrences from formal moment functionals

Put σ=x2−4, and define formal residues at infinity by

ρ1[f]=[x−1]f(x)σ−3/2,ρ2[f]=[x−1]f(x)σ−5/2.

The second functional is the ν of the preceding proofs, and ρ1=σρ2. Their even moments are respectively m(2mm)/2 and m(m−1)(2mm)/12; odd moments vanish.

For n≥3, the monic formal orthogonal polynomials for ρ1 are

qn=σ3/2(2n−3)!/(n−3)!∂xnσn−3/2.

The Rodrigues expression is monic, and formal integration by parts gives orthogonality. More explicitly, its norm is

ρ1[qn2]=ρ1[qnxn]=(−1)nn!(2n−3)!/(n−3)!⋅(−4)n−1(n−3/2n−1)=−2nn−2≠0.

The size-three base Gram determinant is -1. Consequently

HN(ρ1)=(−2)N(N−1)(N−2)16(N≥3).

The operator σ∂x2−x∂x is formally self-adjoint because (σσ−3/2)′=−xσ−3/2. Orthogonality and nonsingularity give σqn″−xqn′=n(n−2)qn. Its monic solution is unique, since the eigenvalue difference at degree j<n is (n−j)(n+j−2)≠0. With x=z+z−1, substitution therefore gives

(n−2)qn(x)=(n−2)Cn(x)−nCn−2(x),Cn(z+z−1)=zn+z−n.

The coefficients of the two exponential branches have degree one in n. These assertions also have separate exact polynomial, orthogonality and norm checks in the replay. The Rodrigues/orthogonality argument is the same formal residue argument as in Theorem K, with the displayed exponent changed; it uses no positive measure.

For a quadratic R=Ax2+Bx+C multiplying ρ1, the two-root augmented-Vandermonde identity therefore has four bases and coefficient degree at most two. Their base polynomial is

X4+2CX3+(4B2−8AC−8A2)X2+8A2CX+16A4.

Indeed, if the two roots are r=z+z−1, s=w+w−1, the bases are −2Az±1w±1. Their elementary symmetric functions use r+s=−B/A and rs=C/A, giving the displayed polynomial. Its cube is a uniform order-12 annihilator. The normalization of the raw two-root determinant is (−2A)N/16. Its initial indices one and two agree with the actual determinants by coefficient identities; its value at zero is 1/2. For even R, the four branches give three distinct bases generically, so the bound improves to nine. The resulting characteristic factor for u=1 is the previously published (X−2a)(X2−4(a−b)X+4a2); scaling the functional by u scales every exponential base by u.

For a quadratic multiplying ρ2, use the raw polynomials Pn=(n−3)(n−4)pn from Theorem K. The normalization is

(2A)N(N−1)(N−2)4608.

The determinant of two raw branches has coefficient degree at most four; the extra factor has degree two. Thus four bases give the uniform bound 28, with seventh powers of

X4−2CX3+(4B2−8AC−8A2)X2−8A2CX+16A4.

Indices one through four are exact coefficient identities, using the same low raw polynomials as Theorem L; the zero-index continuation is 1/8.

Each coefficient has degree at most six, so their seventh powers give a uniform order-42 recurrence. Here i2=−1 is used in an algebraic extension only; the resulting characteristic polynomial has coefficients in the original field. For d=av, r2=4−6b/a, it is

[(X2+4a2v2){X4+(8a2−96ab+144b2)v2X2+16a4v4}]7.

For the initial boundary, divide the raw polynomials by the monic cubic x3−r2x and take the three-by-three remainder coefficient determinant. The identities at indices one through four agree coefficientwise with the actual moment determinants. At zero the continuation is 1/4.

For all three constructions, the generic calculation takes place where the displayed root determinants are nonsingular. For each fixed recurrence index, the residue is a polynomial in the original coefficients. Thus the identities extend to all specializations, including repeated roots and degree drops. No inverse singular minor or limiting inference from numeric roots is used.

The normalizations above omit two nonzero boundary intersections. Their closed expressions, for N≥1, are

Each nonzero family's reduced numerator has the same degree as its reduced denominator; their leading coefficient ratio is nonzero. Consequently the reduced recurrence starts at one and cannot include index zero. The exponential continuations at zero are 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 or 1/16, depending on the stratum, whereas the actual empty determinant is always one. Zero functionals give WN=0 for N≥1, also with the start at one.

This completes the coordinate-boundary classification using the written derivations and the replayed coefficientwise certificate leaves. Those leaves are finite polynomial identities with proved coverage bounds, not sampled evidence for an infinite pattern. Review remains project self-review; historical novelty, independent review and Lean formalization are unassessed.

N.2. The sixteen bases and their leading coefficients

For a rowwise choice vi∈{zi,zi−1}, define

N.3. All collisions with simple roots

The nonzero hypotheses give

(N7)R(2)=12tw,R(−2)=−12tw.

No two distinct roots of R can be opposites. Indeed, if r,−r were roots with r≠0, the even and odd parts of (N1), with σ=r2−4, would give σ(σ+2t)=0 and σ+6t=0. Their combination is 24t2=0, a contradiction. A zero root occurs only at t=2; its derivative is 8w≠0, so it is always simple.

Two sign vertices at Hamming distance one can collide only if some zi2=1, contradicting (N7). At distance two, the condition is (ziϵizjϵj)2=1, which would give equal or opposite roots. Thus a collision has distance three or four. There cannot be a cluster of three vertices: relative to one vertex, two distinct flip sets of sizes at least three have symmetric difference of size at most two. Every cluster therefore has size at most two.

For a distance-three pair put v1v2v3=e, e∈{1,−1}. Inverting these three branches changes the ratio of (N5) by

Every factor is nonzero: a zero factor would be a zero branch or an endpoint root. Thus the aggregate coefficient still has degree six.

For distance four, put V=∏ivi. Directly from (N5), A(v−1)=VA(v). At a positive full collision, V=1, the leading terms add. At a negative full collision, V=−1, they cancel. Since S(v−1)=−4−S(v), (N6) gives the retained degree-five coefficient

Both identities in (N9) are checked over Q[t,q]. There is exactly one cluster at the negative base when it occurs. Every other distinct base contributes order seven, and that one contributes six. This proves 7h−δ for simple roots, including every intersection of their collision conditions.

N.4. What confluence does to a coefficient degree

Suppose a root of multiplicity m is split formally as r+e1,…,r+em, and choose a local branch z, with r=z+z−1. Its logarithmic derivative is α=1/(z−z−1)≠0. Choose k of the plus branches and m−k inverse branches. In the denominator following (N5), exactly the k(m−k) cross-branch factors vanish. Each has linear part α(ei−ej), with i in the plus set and j outside it. All other factors have nonzero limits.

Group the choices of the plus set before taking the confluent divided difference. This grouped numerator is alternating in the root variables, so division by their Vandermonde is regular. Every coefficient of Ln is Laurent polynomial, and hence has no further poles. Consequently the coefficient degree can increase by at most d=k(m−k).

The leading coefficient increases by exactly d. To see that it does not cancel, take the leading degree-six term and expand its exponential factor. Up to a common nonzero factor, the required local limit is

∑I⊆{1,…,m}#I=kexp⁡(τ∑i∈Iei)∏i∈I, j∉I(ei−ej),τ=2αn.

For the multiplicities needed here, its value at all ei=0 is

(m,k)Local value
(2,1)τ
(3,1)τ2/2
(3,2)τ2/2

These identities are algebraic divided differences. The first is (eτe1−eτe2)/(e1−e2). The second is its second divided difference, whose coincident value is the quadratic Taylor coefficient τ2/2. For the third, use the complement of the two-element set; the expression becomes eτ∑ei times the second divided difference of e−τx, with the same value. This uses only finite Taylor coefficients over a characteristic-zero field. It does not use an analytic limit or an assumption about positive measures.

All common factors are nonzero, including α and the nonvanishing factors of (N5). Lower powers of n have the same pole bound and cannot cancel this highest power. Thus the exact degree of this grouped coefficient is

6+k(m−k).

For several repeated roots the contributions add; in particular two double roots give degree 6+k1(2−k1)+k2(2−k2).

After this confluence, the coefficient functions are regular whenever the distinct root groups stay distinct and avoid the endpoints. Further spectral collisions therefore combine finite coefficient polynomials; they do not create another degree increase.

N.5. A double root and every collision on its locus

Let the roots be r,r,s,t0. The double root is nonzero, by (N7) and the zero-root derivative calculation. There are eight modes in which its two branches have the same sign; call these the A modes. They have degree six and their leading coefficients are the regular repeated-entry values of (N5). The four mixed-sign modes from that double root, the B modes, have bases 2auzs±1zt0±1 and degree seven.

The four B bases are distinct and none is ±2au: otherwise the two simple roots would be equal or opposite, or an endpoint would occur. A collision involving B and one or more A modes retains degree seven, because only one B mode belongs to each such cluster.

An A-only cluster has at most two modes. Regard an A sign vector as a four-bit vector with its first two bits equal. A distance-two collision that flips those first two bits would require zr4=1, hence r∈{0,2,−2}, all excluded. The other distance-one and distance-two collisions were already excluded in subsection N.3. The same binary-code argument therefore applies. Distance-three pairs retain degree six; the calculation in subsection N.3 permits repeated entries in (N5). A positive full pair also retains degree six. The negative full pair has exact degree five by (N8); the symmetric identities proving its nonvanishing also permit repeated entries.

Exactly four of the h clusters contain B modes. Their contributions are eight each, and the others contribute seven, except for the one possible negative full pair. Thus the order is

4⋅8+(h−4)⋅7−δ=7h+4−δ.

This includes intersections of confluence with every spectral collision, without assuming that the discriminant locus is smooth.

N.7. Minimality, coefficient field, and initial index

An exponential polynomial λNp(N), with λ≠0 and deg⁡p=d, has a generating-function pole of exact order d+1 at z=λ−1. Its leading pole coefficient contains the nonzero factor d! times the leading coefficient of p. Distinct bases give distinct poles. Hence the minimal eventual recurrence order is exactly the sum of these d+1, after combining equal bases. This proves the lower bounds as well as the annihilators counted above.

The calculations can be made in a finite splitting field. Permuting roots or inverting the chosen lifts permutes the summands. Consequently the monic minimal annihilator is invariant under the splitting field's Galois group, so it lies in the original field. Its order is unchanged by that extension. Likewise, the gcd degrees in (N3) are unchanged by field extension.

For repeated roots, (N4) uses the rows of derivatives divided by their factorials and the confluent Vandermonde ∏i<j(rj−ri)mimj. The low-index boundary identities of Theorem L are polynomial identities in the quartic coefficients, so they remain valid under this confluence. Equivalently, the initial coefficient determinants are unchanged when evaluations are replaced by these normalized jets. Thus the exponential polynomial gives the actual WN for every N≥1. Its continuation at zero is still 1/2, by the same degree-three boundary determinant as in Theorem L.

Every base is nonzero. The minimal annihilator therefore has nonzero constant coefficient, and its residual at zero is half that coefficient, since the actual empty determinant is one. The recurrence cannot be extended to index zero without increasing its order. This completes the stated classification.

The separate standard-library replay verifies the nine characteristic coefficient lists on 45 degree-complete parameter nodes. At coefficient index j≤8, homogeneity gives degree at most j in t and at most j in w; evenness in w gives degree at most ⌊j/2⌋ in q. The 9-by-5 grid therefore proves coefficient coverage; reciprocal symmetry supplies the other coefficients. The ten sample GFs are reconstructed under Theorem L's all-index bound and have exact cross-multiplication and degree-preserving modular Bezout certificates. Their parameter interpolation uses 57 distinct squared nodes, covering the proved degree at most 56 in q through W112. The finite confluence regressions independently use rational lifted roots, polynomial jets, and actual monomial determinants. Those regression quartics need not belong to the mixed family; their orders are checks of the mechanism.

Finite samples alone do not prove this theorem. Universal coverage follows the collision and confluence arguments above and the coefficientwise leaves with their proved bounds. Section 7 states the remaining broader scope.

6. Certificates and reproduction

6.1. How a finite certificate proves an all-index assertion

The written proofs supply the uniform annihilators and their start indices. Finite determinant values alone would not supply those conclusions. For clarity, the algebraic bridge used by the generating-function certificates is recorded here.

Certificate lemma. Suppose a sequence satisfies a monic recurrence A(S)WN=0 of order r for every N≥1. Set

(E2)G(z)=∑N≥0WNzN,D(z)=zrA(z−1),H(z)=[D(z)G(z)]≤r.

Then D(0)=1 and G=H/D. The numerator H is determined by W0,…,Wr. If proposed polynomials U,V, with V(0)=1, satisfy UD=HV, then G=U/V. If they are coprime, its reduced denominator has degree deg⁡V, which is exactly the minimal eventual scalar constant-coefficient recurrence order.

Proof. The coefficient of zN+r in DG is the stated recurrence residual. Thus every coefficient above degree r vanishes, which proves (E2) and the cross-multiplication assertion. If a monic recurrence of order d holds eventually, multiplication of G by its reversed polynomial yields a polynomial. Coprimality of U,V forces V to divide that reversed polynomial, so d≥deg⁡V. Conversely, multiplication by V gives an eventual recurrence of order deg⁡V. This proves equality, including order zero.

The modular witnesses in the source package establish coprimality after clearing rational denominators. They retain both polynomial degrees and verify a Bezout identity equal to one modulo the stated prime. A nonconstant common factor over the rationals would retain a nonconstant common factor under that degree-preserving reduction, contradicting the identity. This supplies an exact lower bound, rather than an inference from a fitted list.

6.2. Portable replay

Extract the current sequence-formula source ZIP into a fresh directory. Python 3.10+ and its standard library suffice for the mathematical replay:

python -B tools/verify_sequence_final_edition.py --output final-edition-checks

The command runs the six retained replayers supporting this edition: the quadratic order-63 sample, the mixed order-112 sample, the sharp uniform quadratic theorem, the uniform mixed theorem, the complete boundary table, and the complete nonzero rule. It checks the component outputs and writes a combined receipt. The original certificates are proposed coefficient lists; the replayers reconstruct and verify their identities.

The N replay includes 45 degree-complete characteristic nodes, eight exact Bezout leaves, ten reduced generating-function certificates, confluence regressions, and 2,732 direct defining determinant comparisons. The written collision and confluence arguments provide universal coverage. Some general quartics in the confluence regressions lie outside the mixed family; those checks do not assert that every regression order occurs in that family.

For an individual normalized parameter, use, for example:

python -B tools/sequence_hankel_orders.py --coefficients verification/sequence-library/hankel-compression/interior-coefficients.json --t 1 --q 1

This returns minimal eventual order 98. For a negative fractional argument, use the equals form, for example --q=-16/9. The browser engine can be compared with the Python engine using the optional Node.js 24 checks:

python -B -m unittest discover -s tools -p test_sequence_hankel_orders.py -v
node --test tools/test_sequence_hankel_orders.mjs

The versioned PDF and standalone HTML are produced from this same manuscript. Their build receipt pins the manuscript, the four imported proof sources, the renderer, and the output hashes. PDF rendering uses the retained MathJax SVG runtime and a Chromium browser; it is separate from the standard-library mathematical replay. Typography may vary with a different rendering engine.

6.3. Source lineage and review

This edition is based on source revision af2d91ead77d06f7903239f1da293e26bb00f240 and its 101-member source archive, whose SHA-256 is e7a43e634553bf7d814518cd65a14769a2d2094afd8db85e5641675afca52ccd. That archive is retained unchanged as sequence-formula-source-af2d91ea.zip. The predecessor mathematical notes and their certificates remain unchanged. The assembly report records the editorial joins, updated historical scope sentences, and local cross-reference labels used in the consolidated paper. Every imported TeX expression is checked against its source.

The source reviews are retained as SHARP_QUADRATIC_REVIEW.md, UNIFORM_MIXED_REVIEW.md, EXCEPTIONAL_ORDERS_REVIEW.md, and INTERIOR_ORDERS_REVIEW.md. The final-edition review checks their integration, the boundary/nonzero partition, notation, certificate dependencies, and the new certificate lemma. These are project self-reviews. Automated code tests, browser checks, and source hashes serve their stated purposes; they do not constitute independent mathematical review or Lean formalization.

7. Scope of the final edition

The mixed linear-weight, first-order-operator minimal-order classification is complete as stated by Theorems M and N, with Theorem L giving the optimal uniform bound. The quadratic identity-operator bound in Theorem K is also sharp, but it does not classify the minimal order at every quadratic weight. Pointwise quadratic-weight orders, higher-degree weights, and higher-order mixed operators remain separate research targets.

This is a finalized edition of those stated results and their reproducible evidence. It makes no historical novelty claim. Later corrections or extensions should receive a new version while preserving this edition's sources and hashes.
